blocks.text: **The problem.** Implement a last-in-first-out stack using only **queues**. Your class `MyStack` must support `push(x)`, `pop()` (remove and return the top), `top()` (return the top) and `empty()`. You may only use standard queue operations: add to the **back**, remove from the **front**, look at the front, size and is-empty. Calls to `pop` and `top` are always made on a non-empty stack.

blocks.alt: The mismatch. After pushing 1, 2, 3, a stack must hand back 3 first. A queue holding 1, 2, 3 can only hand back 1, the oldest, from its front.

blocks.text: A queue always releases its **oldest** item; a stack must release its **newest**. Every solution is about getting the newest item to the **front** of a queue — either at pop time or at push time.
1. Brute force: dig the newest item out at pop time

Push is easy: add to the back of `q1`. To pop, the newest item is at the **back**, so move every other item from `q1` into a helper queue `q2`, take the last one, then swap the queues' roles. `top()` can reuse `pop()` and put the item back.

blocks.alt: Popping from q1 holding 1, 2, 3: the first two items, 1 and 2, move to q2 in order; 3 is left alone and is returned. Then q2 becomes the main queue.

blocks.text: **push O(1); pop and top O(n); space O(n).** Every pop shuffles the whole queue — painful if the stack is popped or peeked often.
2. Optimal: do the work at push time instead

Flip where the cost goes. Keep `q1` in **newest-first** order at all times, so its front is always the top. To push `x`: put `x` into the **empty** `q2`, move everything from `q1` behind it, then swap. Now `pop` and `top` are a plain dequeue and peek.

blocks.alt: Pushing 4 when q1 holds 3, 2, 1 newest-first. 4 goes into the empty q2, then 3, 2 and 1 follow it, so q2 holds 4, 3, 2, 1. The queues swap names.

blocks.text: **push O(n); pop and top O(1); space O(n).** Usually better than the brute force: most programs read the top more often than they push.
3. Best solution: one queue that rotates

The second queue isn't needed. Push `x` at the back of the **one** queue, then **rotate**: take each of the older items off the front and add it to the back, one by one. After `size - 1` rotations, `x` is at the front and the rest follow newest-first — the same order as the optimal solution, with half the queues.

blocks.alt: Rotating one queue. It holds 3, 2, 1 newest-first. Push 4 at the back: 3, 2, 1, 4. Rotate three times: 3 moves to the back, then 2, then 1. The queue becomes 4, 3, 2, 1, with 4 at the front.

blocks.caption: Each push rotates the older items behind the new one.

blocks.text: **push O(n); pop, top and empty O(1); space O(n) in a single queue.** (In JavaScript, `shift()` on a plain array is itself O(n) for big arrays — here we count queue operations, as the problem intends. A real queue class, like Python's `deque`, does them in O(1).)

rows.approach: Brute force: dig the newest item out at pop time
rows.timeWhy: Pop and top **move every item but the newest** to the other queue.

rows.approach: Optimal: do the work at push time instead
rows.timeWhy: Each push puts the new item **in front of all older ones**, so pop and top are O(1).
Each push **rotates the older items** behind the new one.

items: **A single item** — push then pop: the rotation loop runs zero times.
**pop until empty, then push again** — `empty()` must flip back to false.
**Interleaved push / pop / top** — after every push the newest item must be the one returned.
**Repeated values** — `push 5, push 5, pop`: the order must still be correct.

blocks.text: **Related:** the reverse problem — a **queue built from two stacks** — has a neater trick: items move from one stack to the other only when the second runs dry, which makes every operation O(1) amortized.
